title: Reflections of Relentless Rain
speaker: Kukushin Kate McCandless
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of letting go of our tendency to separate ourselves from the world around us, instead embracing our embodied experience and allowing reality to unfold freely. By doing so, we can observe life more accurately and respond with wisdom and compassion, rather than being controlled by our conditioned perceptions. This understanding can lead to freedom from fixed views and patterns, allowing for a seamless practice of mindfulness and awakening.

sentences.text: Our speaker today is from the sister Sangha in the north, Mountain Rain Zen.
Kukushin Kate McCandless is a co-guiding teacher of Mountain Rain Zen.
We so appreciate that we get to see her, since our border remains closed.
Thank you very much, Kate, for making the virtual trip.
I'd also like to encourage the community to remember that our teachers do not get paid for their various appearances.
If you wish to give dana to Kate and Mountain Rain Zen, please visit the website and the donation page there.
Thank you very much.
Well, good morning, everyone.
How wonderful to see your faces.
I was trying to remember the last time we were in Bellingham.
I'm sure you've experienced how warpy time is lately, so I don't trust my memory very well.
But it feels like it might have been in early March, right before lockdown last year.
Was it when Michael did his guest talk?
I'm not sure, but it doesn't matter.
It's been a long time since that border has been closed.

I'm really looking forward to the day when not only that border but so many borders and so many barriers and walls that have been erected in so many different ways dissolve and come down, and we can move freely in our lives again.
But we have to be patient.
It's not quite around the corner yet.
And how wonderful that we've been able to continue practicing in these weird virtual ways.
Who would have imagined a year ago that we would be doing this?
Not in our dreams did we know we'd be doing this.
Anyway, it's so lovely to see your faces.
At Mountain Rain we ramped up within a week to put everything on Zoom.
It was quite something.
What's even so sweet is seeing people's home altars.
We're going to assemble an album of home altars, to share and to remind us how courageous we've all been to continue practicing in this way in our little grass hut zendos.
Before I launch into the talk itself, I want to congratulate you on your new president and administration.

I want to thank all of you for whatever you have been able to do and will continue to do to ensure that the United States finds a way forward from this terrible year with integrity, clarity, respect and justice.
To a very small extent you are able to contribute to that.
You do it for all beings, for the whole world, and for us on this side of the border.
So thank you, Chris, thank you all of you for inviting me.
I asked Chris if there was a topic or some guideline for what I should talk about, and she said, "Well, just talk about practice realization."
I thought, well, that's pretty much everything.
And how wonderful that our practice does include pretty much everything.
It's all inclusive.
But then I realized that your shuso, Joden Bob, has chosen Shitou's song of the grass roof hermitage for your practice period theme.
Am I correct on that?
Has it actually begun?
Yes, okay, good.
I thought this is great, because of course we've all been doing a lot of grass hut practice, our solitary grass hut practice.
Some of us more solitary, some of us trying to practice with family members, kids, dogs and cats running around the house.
One thing about grass huts is you can always hear the rain on the roof.
Sometimes it comes [unclear: "troops"].
How many of you woke to the sound of rain this morning?
Anybody?
It was soft, I think, and here it was actually snow.
Anybody else have snow?
Yeah, Hannah would do this.
Yeah, we have light snow, I think it's already turning to rain.
One thing I decided I want to share with you was some reflections from last week, when the rain was feeling kind of relentless, or maybe it was a little earlier than last week.
There have been different times when the rain has felt pretty relentless this winter, even though that's typical for our part of the world.
I wasn't sure if my perception was skewed by a touch of cabin fever at that point.
So I actually looked up the records of monthly precipitation in Vancouver.
And yes indeed, November and December, just this past, were higher than the previous year.
January of last year was record-breaking precipitation, and if the second half of this January equals the first half, it will be record-breaking again.
Yeah, there's been a lot of rain.
Not only that, the storms.
We have storms in recent years that seem more intense, with more violent wind.
Is that my imagination?
Anybody else think so?
I do.
Yeah, sometimes short, violent, intense, like monsoon.
I guess it was Tuesday of the week before, in the middle of the night, there was this just violent wind and rain, and it woke me up.
In the morning I looked out in the backyard, and there was a big hemlock tree fallen across our whole backyard.
I think that's what woke me, the sound of that, not only the rain and the wind but that tree going down.
They shake the earth when they go down, those big trees.
The soil has been so saturated that the big hemlocks and cedars with their shallow roots can just peel right off.
I'm sure maybe you've seen some of that if you've been out walking in the forest.

At times that stormy weather has seemed to mirror the storms raging in the political and social atmosphere this past year, also seemingly relentless, threatening to destabilize a sense of groundedness and connection.
I'm sure you've all felt that.
The old Japanese haiku poets often wrote of weathering winter rain and storms in their solitary huts.
The poet Isa wrote:
*Winter seclusion.* *That evening, listening to mountain rain.*
I thought maybe we should put that one on our website.
And Basho wrote:
*Winter solitude, in a world of one color.* *The sound of wind.*
Just that.
The sound of wind.
Sometimes winter rain evokes loneliness and isolation.
The haiku poet Buson wrote:
*Huddled in here for the winter.* *My heart is far away from the Buddha.*
We feel kind of distant from our practice, especially when we can't gather for sangha potlucks and hugs.
But the poet writes it just as it is: just this loneliness this evening.
And in attending to it, it's that and more.
Then inexplicably we hear the same sound of rain and come alive.
Another poet, Shoho, wrote:
*To wake alive in this world.* *What happiness.
Winter rain.*
Same rain, same sound.
More rain.
Put on your gumboots and raincoat.
Go out in the garden.
Dig some parsnips and leeks for dinner.
Smell the earth.
Rinse it from the roots.
Receive their nourishment.
All this is preamble to a koan that I was reminded of, from the Blue Cliff Record, case 46, a dialogue between Zen master Qingjing and a monk.
Qingjing asks the monk:
*What's that sound outside the gate?*
The monk replies:
*Sound of raindrops.*
And Qingjing says:
*Sentient beings are inverted.
They lose themselves and follow after things.*
Then the monk asks:
*What about you, teacher?*
And his teacher replies:
*I almost don't lose myself.*
The monk asks:
*What is the meaning of "I almost don't lose myself"?*
And his teacher says:
*Though it still should be easy to express oneself, to say the whole thing has to be difficult.*
Well, I'll second that.
To say the whole thing is virtually impossible.
That's why we have haiku: to say something about one moment that includes and applies to all the rest.
What's that sound outside the gate?
Qingjing asks us.
Right now, what do you hear?
Outside?
Inside?
The sound of raindrops.
A tree crashing to the ground.
A raging mob pounding on the door.
Your own heart pounding an alarm.
Voices of hatred and vengeance.
Voices of calm and kindness.
Qingjing tells us, "Sentient beings are inverted.
They lose themselves and follow after things."
So what's he saying?
Another translation says, "Sentient beings have it backwards."
In the Heart Sutra, there's that line, *far beyond all inverted views*.
So: inverted, upside down, backwards views.
They're those habitual ways that we see ourselves as a separate entity, in opposition, cut off, us against the world or us outside the world, the world outside us, self and other.
In a way, we stubbornly refuse to see that our being is a dynamic, changing process, always in relationship to everything else.
And so we lose ourselves, right?
We lose ourselves and follow after things.
The things that we believe will confirm our existence and make us feel whole and make us feel worthy.
Of course, this doesn't just mean material things, does it?
It means the approval, the recognition, the success we crave.
Another translation says, "They don't see their own body and chase after things."
I wish I'd taken the time to look up the original and see what the original phrase is.
This sense that we lose touch with our own embodied experience makes sense to me.
We don't open our sense gates, our eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body and mind, and allow the 10,000 things to reveal themselves to us, right?
We're not in touch with our own embodied experience.
Instead we go out reaching, reaching, reaching for the things as though they're out there somewhere.
Many of you, I'm sure, know Dogen's quintessential lines:
*To carry yourself forward and experience myriad things is delusion.
That myriad things come forth and experience themselves is awakening.*

So he's making that contrast between the way we chase after things instead of meeting things, allowing the things of the world to come forth in their being, and for us to meet them just as they are, just as each moment is.
And Dogen continues, I think with a touch of rueful humor:
*Those who have great realization of delusion are Buddhas, and those who are greatly deluded about realization are sentient beings.*
So the monk in the koan realizes how hard it is to let go of his inverted views, and he asks his teacher, "What about you?"
You think it's easy?
What about you?
And Qingjing replies, "I almost don't lose myself," which is such a beautifully simple, humble and accurate reply.
Who among us maintains a perfectly enlightened view all the time?
Raise your hand if you think you do.
Not me.
Maybe there are a few alive who come close.
His Holiness the Dalai Lama, maybe a few.
But the thing is, if we are to live as bodhisattvas in this world of suffering, it's good that we know what it feels like to be deluded.
It's good that we can sit and be awake in our delusion.
In doing this, Dogen says we are Buddhas.
And in doing this, we keep our hearts open to suffering beings, so we don't hold ourselves above.
But the monk is still puzzled.
He says, "What do you mean you almost don't lose yourself?"
Isn't his teacher supposed to be an exemplar of enlightenment?
We don't like it when our teachers aren't perfect.
And his teacher replies, "Though it should be easy to express oneself, to say the whole thing has to be difficult."
So even after decades of practice, shouldn't it be easy to just manifest our practice, just express ourselves fully?
But the old teacher says this is really beyond words.
We try to express our experience of the sound outside the gate or the door of our heart, but our words do not say the whole thing.
They're fingers pointing at the moon, as the old saying goes.
So really, we can only do our best to actualize our practice in every moment of our daily lives, never resting on our laurels.
As Dogen says, being greatly deluded about enlightenment, we assume it's a once-and-for-all proposition that will solve all our problems and remove all obstacles for good.
No, it's ongoing commitment to practice, to purifying karma, to letting go of hindrances and entering each moment.
There's another short Zen dialogue that resonates with this one.
This time, it's a monk and his teacher, Xuan Xia, who was a dharma brother of Qingjing in the previous story.
The monk has just arrived at the monastery to practice for the first time with his master.
He introduces himself and says, "I have just entered this monastery.
Please show me where to enter the way."
And Xuan Xia asks him, "Do you hear the sound of the stream in the valley?"
"Yes," said the monk.
"Enter there," says Xuan Xia.
So here again is the Zen master using sound as a dharma gate.
Enter there right now.
Rain lashing the window, a towering red cedar crashing to the ground, an angry mob, a child's cry, a rising, a passing.
What's your reply?
Notice how each one of these sounds can be aversive or pleasurable or neutral.
It's simply a sound with a unique quality arising and subsiding.
Depending on the conditions, your reaction to exactly the same sound will be different.
So is that dog barking your beloved pet who's delighted that you've just come home?
Or is it your neighbor's dog yapping when you're trying to concentrate?
Or is that child's cry a cry of surprise or delight or fear or pain?
You might not even be able to tell which it is if it's at a little bit of a distance.
But your own conditioning and associations with that sound of the child's cry will affect how you perceive it.
Or even whether you notice it at all.
If you're absorbed in your own concerns or you have your headphones on, you might not even hear that child's cry.
And is that shouting mob angry because their favorite team lost, or cheering because they won?
At a distance, you can't even tell.
Is the sound outside the temple gate inside or outside, inside your mind?

So when we begin to really pay attention to sound and our perception of sounds, we begin to notice how similar that process is to our perception of everything: other sensory information, or our perception of our own mind's content.
And this is why listening practice is such a good template for seeing into the nature of mind, for observing memories, daydreams, worries, all those inner dialogues that run in our mind.
They arise and subside, just like the rain on the roof.
Sometimes it's really stormy.
Our reactions are conditioned as well and have no objective reality.
So we can, again, experience our reactions just as we do the sounds.
It doesn't mean that we ignore the world around us.
But the freedom from [unclear: "reaching"] self clinging removes the distortions that cloud our vision and distort our perception of the world around us, and impair our hearing.
And then we can observe as accurately as possible and respond as appropriately as possible with wise and compassionate means.
As you know, each koan in the Blue Cliff Record is accompanied by a verse by Shuedo, who compiled the collection from older sources.
He compiled it in the 11th century, but most of the sources were a couple of hundred years prior.
And then Yuan Wu, another hundred years later, added commentary.
So there are layers in these koan collections.
Yuan Wu in the commentary tells us that Qingjing used this same question.
So this is apparently a question he used with his students.
He asked the same question, "What is that sound outside the gate?", to a different monk.
That monk replied, "The sound of a quail."
And Qingjing said, "If you wish to avoid uninterrupted hell, don't slander the wheel of the true Dharma of the Tathagata."
Yikes.
And then he asked it again, the same question, "What is the sound outside the gate?", to a different monk.
And that monk said, "The sound of a snake eating a frog."
And this time, Qingjing replied, "I knew that sentient beings suffered.
Here's another suffering sentient being."
Such different answers each time.
We can't know what about each monk's manner of replying elicited such different responses.
But in the commentary, Yuan Wu says:
*If patchrobed monks can penetrate here, nothing can block their independence within the heaps of sound and form.
If you can't penetrate, then you are constrained by sound and form.*

When he's referring to the heaps of sound and form, he's referring to the five skandhas, the aggregates that we chant in the Heart Sutra: form, sensations, perceptions, mental formations and consciousness.
It's a model in Buddhist thought of how we function as conscious beings.
The Heart Sutra, of course, tells us that these five skandhas are empty, meaning that they don't have separate, substantial, permanent existence, that they exist only as a dynamic interrelationship.
And when we deeply understand this, Yuan Wu is telling us, when we live this understanding, we are not constrained by our fixed views and our conditioned habit patterns.
Practice, realization and actualization are seamless.
In the introduction to this koan, Yuan Wu says:
*His slightest word can break things up, untying what is bound and releasing what is stuck, as if walking on thin ice or running over sword blades.
He sits within the heaps of sound and form.
He walks on top of sound and form.*

So it's a poetic description of the freedom of living in a world of sound and form, and suffering, with this freedom, this freedom of the unencumbered mind, sitting within heaps of sound and form, walking on top of sound and form.
Living in this world, so much going on, so much going on, not being hooked or snagged by our conditioned mind.
So the verse for this koan goes like this:
*An empty hall, the sound of raindrops.
Hard to respond, even for an adept.
If you say he's let the streams enter, as before you still don't understand.
Understanding or not understanding.
On North South Mountain, on North Mountain, more and more downpour.*
Yuan Wu comments on that line, "understanding or not understanding," saying there's relative and absolute.
There's letting go and gathering in.
There's killing and bringing to life.
There's catching and releasing.
This is how we awaken: practicing right in the middle of the cacophony of life, entering the Dharma gate of each moment.
Even if that moment is our aversion and our frustration, we enter that.
We catch our delusion and release it.
I love the catch and release image.
That's what we do even in our zazen: catch and release.
The great 20th-century Rinzai Zen master Hakuun Yasutani Roshi wrote this poem:
*Just listening, body having no self.
The raindrops falling from the eaves of the house are nothing if not myself.*
Sound of raindrops, the waterfall in the mountain valley, the dog barking next door, the mob outside the gate.
Nothing if not myself.
Now it might be hard to say that about the mob, right?
We want to think of them as not me.
Definitely not me, not us.
People are saying this.
You're hearing this.
"This is not America.
This is not America."
But there's a danger in that denial.
When we really look deeply into the mind of greed, hatred and delusion, we see that none of us is exempt.
We share the common roots of delusion with all humankind.
What part of yourself would you rather keep outside the door, outside the gate, and not listen to?
Jungian psychology calls those parts our shadow.
We might say the American shadow has been raging for attention.
What's it saying?
When you're a parent of an adolescent who's screaming at you in narcissistic rage, making accusations that are so exaggerated, I don't know if anyone's ever had that experience.
I haven't, but I've heard about it.
When the kid just screams at you, and it's all you can do not to scream back, or maybe you do scream back, saying, "Can't you see how much I care about you?"
And they say, "You don't care about me.
If you did, you'd..." fill in the blank: do what they want.
How do you respond?
How can we respond to rage with clarity and firmness and kindness and integrity?
That's about as hard as practice gets, I think: confronting rage.
I was thinking, actually, about what's been going on in the U.S.
And excuse me, don't think I'm trying to be a superior Canadian here.
I was born and raised in New Jersey, so I take all this deeply to heart and have for decades.
But it struck me that what's been going on in America is more like sibling rivalry.
You know, who has the advantage, who has the disadvantage, who's being neglected, who's been given too much, that kind of mentality.
Old grievances passed down through generations.
And for so long, there's been a lot of shouting and not enough listening going on.
At Mountain Rain Zen, we've been having monthly meetings of our engaged practice group.
And we've had discussions about what our practice has to offer for those engaged in social and environmental justice.
I would say our practice offers a perspective on the roots of suffering.
And it offers practices that support harmonious and respectful relationships between human beings, and with other sentient beings that live on this earth with us.
I would say our practice offers us the capacity for deep listening and for responding with speech and action guided by wisdom and compassion.
In our practice period, we studied the paramitas and we added bonus paramitas.
We added about four or five extras.
And all of them are just the very practices, not abstract qualities, but practices that sustain us through this time.
And this is what our practice has to offer for engaging in this world.
Remember the name Kanzeon, we chanted just now, Kanzeon, the Bodhisattva of compassion.
Her name means the one who hears the cries of the world.
So again, listening.
The other thing our practice gives us is the patience and steadfastness to almost not lose ourselves.
And when we lose ourselves, which we will over and over again, to find our way home again and again.
And sometimes it takes a long time.
One day, a rainy day at Green Gulch Temple, the poet Gary Snyder told this story.
I wasn't there.
The story has been passed around.
Years ago when Gary Snyder was a young man studying Zen in Japan, he attended a practice period during the rainy season.
And if you've ever been to Japan in the rainy season, it's just relentless downpour.
Every afternoon there was a Dharma talk by the Roshi, and this fierce monsoon rainstorm would come down, and the Roshi had a faint little voice and they could never hear him.
It went on like this day after day.
They could not hear the talk.
And years later, Gary met a man who had attended that same practice period with him, and the guy said, "You remember all those Dharma talks we couldn't hear the whole time?
Well, I'm beginning to hear them now.
Raindrops on the roof."
I'm beginning to hear them now.
Raindrops on the roof.
The cries of sentient beings in pain or delight.
Nothing but yourself.
That is the way a Bodhisattva perceives the sounds of the world.
That is the way a beginner Bodhisattva enters the way.
Right here, right now.
In the sound of this moment.
I have no inside.
So that's all I'll say.
I just want to encourage you to really take up listening practice.
I find it always inexhaustibly refreshing of my practice to do listening practice.
So I guess we don't chat.
I will just thank you, thank you, thank you for showing up today, and for your ongoing practice, and may the day come when we can not only sit together in the zendo, but share good food again.
That's the thing we really, really miss, isn't it?
Thanks, folks.
What happens next, Chris?
I would like to invite people to unmute.
And we can have a conversation and explore what came up during Kate's Dharma talk and our own experience.
So please feel free to unmute and speak, speak.
You know, I would also just be really happy to hear about what your experience has been practicing through these times, south of the border.
I mean, maybe you're all talked out.
